subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Cultural Variation in Fairness
description: A fast breakdown of Cultural Variation in Fairness for builders.

hook.text: In the ultimatum game, Americans offer 45%. The Machiguenga of Peru offer 15%. Same game, radically different norms.

buildup.text: Henrich ran the ultimatum game across 15 small-scale societies. Offers ranged from 15% to 58%. Culture shapes fairness.

discovery.text: Societies with more market integration made fairer offers. Trade experience teaches equal exchange as a norm.

twist.text: The Lamelara whale hunters gave more than 50%. Their survival depends on sharing. Ecology shapes economic norms.

climax.text: Fairness is not a universal instinct with a fixed setting. It is shaped by culture, ecology, and economic experience.

punchline.text: Fairness is universal. What counts as fair is not.

quiz.question: What did Henrich's cross-cultural ultimatum game studies show?
options: Market integration correlates with fairer offers
No culture shows fairness in economic games

details.summary: Experiments like the Ultimatum Game reveal dramatic cultural variation in fairness norms. Some cultures routinely offer 50-50 splits, others offer less, and some offer more than half. Market integration and community cooperation predict fairness norms better than wealth.
details.whyItMatters: Universal economic models assuming consistent fairness preferences across populations are wrong. Policy and business strategies must account for cultural variation in what people consider fair treatment in economic exchanges.
takeaways: Fairness norms vary dramatically across societies worldwide
Market-integrated societies tend to develop stronger fairness norms
Community cooperation patterns predict economic fairness behavior

faq.question: How do fairness norms vary across cultures?
faq.answer: In ultimatum games across 15 small-scale societies, offers ranged from 15 to 58 percent of the total. Some groups punished both unfair and hyper-generous offers. These variations correlated with the degree of market exchange and cooperative institutions.

faq.question: Why do market-based societies have stronger fairness norms?
faq.answer: Repeated market transactions require trust and reciprocity to function. Societies with more market exchange develop stronger norms of fair dealing because unfair individuals get excluded from future trades, creating evolutionary pressure toward fairness.
